# holt — THE ORDINARY-WORK CORPUS.
#
# Every line is a command that MUST be allowed silently. A false positive here is as serious as
# a missed destroyer: a guard that interrupts work it could have read gets switched off, which
# costs ALL of the protection rather than some of it. Nine interruptions and one save is the
# profile of a guard people uninstall.
#
# THESE ARE NOT INVENTED. Provenance is marked per section:
#   repo             — holt's own package.json scripts, .github/workflows run: steps, and docs
#   readonly         — the dry-run / usage spellings of the verbs holt guards (the [G5] class)
#   journal          — commands the LIVE hook refused during real sessions on the author's
#                      machine, read out of .git/holt/journal.jsonl and adjudicated safe
#   toolchain        — documented invocations of node, python, rust, go, docker, make, kubectl,
#                      terraform and day-to-day git
#   history-shapes   — shapes mined from a real developer's fish/bash/zsh history, with private
#                      paths genericised so they reproduce on any machine
#
# Lines starting with # are comments. Blank lines are ignored.
# Pinned by test/e2e/no-op-invocations.test.mjs, which fails if ANY line is not allowed.

# --- find, xargs and the git pathspec shapes the "not an operand" repair added (48) ---
# find with a destructive ACTION is only as broad as the filters holt can read. Every line here
# names paths that are build output or absent, which is what these commands are for. Parity rule:
# each of these must get the SAME verdict `rm` would get for the same paths.
find . -name "*.pyc" -delete
find . -type f -name "*.pyc" -delete
find . -name "*.pyo" -delete
find . -name "*.orig" -delete
find . -name "*.rej" -delete
find . -name ".DS_Store" -delete
find . -name "*.o" -delete
find . -name "*.class" -delete
find build -type f -delete
find dist -name "*.map" -delete
find target -name "*.rlib" -delete
find . -name "__pycache__" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +
find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm -f {} \;
find coverage -type f -exec rm -f {} +
find . -name "*.o" -print0 | xargs -0 rm -f
find . -name "*.tmp" -print | xargs rm -f
find . -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete
find . -type f -name "*.bak" -delete
# find with no destructive action at all is a read, and always was.
find . -name "*.mjs"
find . -type f -name "*.json" -maxdepth 3
find . -name "*.mjs" -exec grep -l TODO {} +
find . -type d -name node_modules -prune -o -name "*.mjs" -print
find src -name "*.ts" -newer package.json
find . -name "*.mjs" -exec wc -l {} +
find . -name "*.sh" -exec chmod +x {} +
find . -name "*.mjs" -exec git add {} +
# xargs whose utility destroys nothing is untouched, whatever it reads.
find . -name "*.mjs" | xargs grep -l TODO
git ls-files | xargs wc -l
ls | xargs -n1 basename
find . -type f -name "*.json" | xargs -n1 jq -e . > /dev/null
git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -c ''
find . -name "*.mjs" -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 node --check
# the usage and dry-run spellings the option-aware walk must keep silent
git clean -fdx -h
git clean -fdxh
git clean -hfdx
git clean -x -f -d -h
git clean -fdx --help
git checkout -h
git restore -h
git rm -h
git switch -h
git reset --hard -h
git reset --mixed -h
# `-n` is a real dry run even when `-e` eats the `-h` after it. MEASURED: git prints
# "Would remove …" and removes nothing. The option-aware walk is what tells the two apart.
git clean -ne -h -fd
git clean -neh -fd
# an index-only restore loses nothing, in both spellings
git restore --staged src
git restore -S src
git restore --staged --source=HEAD .
# branch work is not a pathspec
git checkout -b feature/x
git checkout -B feature/x origin/main
git switch -c feature/x
git switch main
git checkout --track origin/feature
